docs.title: Record labels are in a spin over AI music
docs.text:
Global 
 Record labels are in a spin over AI music
 The Economist , The Economist 11 min read 6 Oct 2026, 03:56 PM IST 
 Summary
 Should they fight upstart labs, or co-operate with them? 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 THE MUSIC industry is no stranger to technological upheaval. From vinyl to cassettes to CDs to streaming, the recording and selling of music has been in a state of constant revolution. The shift to streaming shook the industry hardest. After the rise of illicit file-sharing in the Napster era, which eventually gave way to legal streaming, it took more than 20 years for revenue to return, even in nominal terms, to the level of the 1990s (see chart 1). Generative artificial intelligence brings a new age of disruption. It threatens to transform the whole process of making music itself.
 Music made by AI is already making its presence felt, in the zeitgeist as “slop” as well as in the charts. There is more dross than ever. Alexis Lanternier, boss of Paris-based Deezer, says that about 90,000 fully machine-generated tunes a day are uploaded to his music-streaming service—half the total. Spotify, the biggest streamer, says it has taken down 75m “spammy tracks” in the past year. Much of the slop is uploaded illegally by bot farms hoping to harvest fraudulent royalties. But many human artists use AI legitimately, to enhance their creativity. “It’s like Ozempic,” says Mr Lanternier. “Everybody is using it, but no one wants to say.”
 A bigger question is the legality of AI-made music itself. Some record labels accuse AI-music labs of piracy and have sued. Some have settled, hoping to make more money from licensing than from lawsuits. Confusingly, some do both. As Mark Mulligan of MIDiA Research, a consultancy, puts it, all are grappling with the problem of how to stay in control of the industry when the ability to create music with AI lowers barriers to entry. Many top music executives cut their teeth (and their first record contracts) in the Napster era. They do not want to get caught napping again.
 The stock market suggests investors are worried. The share prices of the two biggest listed record labels, Universal Music Group (UMG) and Warner Music Group (WMG), have lagged behind the overall market over the past few years (see chart 2). (Sony Music, which ranks between them in revenue, is unlisted.) The relationships to watch are those between all the big labels and Suno, a controversial four-year-old American AI-music company last valued at $5.4bn (more than a third of WMG’s $14.2bn market capitalisation). This presents an intriguing natural experiment: UMG and Sony Music have sued Suno, doubling down with a case filed in September; WMG, having been part of the original suit, has settled.
 In their new case UMG, Sony Music and others accuse Suno of ripping off more than 60,000 copyrighted recordings, by artists from Avril Lavigne to Justin Timberlake, and ingesting them into its models. Under American copyright law damages can reach $150,000 per work, which may suggest the plaintiffs are pushing for a big payout (or exerting pressure to secure a juicy licensing deal).
 Suno admits that the tens of millions of recordings used to train its models include copyrighted material. But it argues that it is “fair use” in law to learn musical styles and generate new, original music. The matter is unsettled: those in the creative industries have more than 100 lawsuits in America against AI labs, including Anthropic and OpenAI, many of which turn on whether fair use applies.
 While the Suno cases go through the courts, WMG’s settlement is also attracting attention. The label has told investors that revenues from its AI partnerships will start flowing this financial year. They would be among the first AI deals in the entertainment industry to bring in real money. Robert Kyncl, boss of WMG, says the firm’s decision to settle with Suno was based on expediency: it might take years for the courts to rule on fair use. “If I can get a partner to give up their fair-use argument and start paying us, why would I wait?” he says.
 The settlement itself may also herald big changes. In September, for instance, Suno introduced v6, which it says is its first family of models to be trained exclusively on licensed music from WMG and others. Artists and songwriters who opt in will share revenues with Suno when their work is used, based on Suno’s subscriptions. Mr Kyncl expects it to yield new revenue streams for artists, as fans create and post AI music derived from remixes or mashups of their repertoires. As an example, he suggests Fleetwood Mac’s “Dreams” overlaid with Aretha Franklin’s voice. “It just brings people joy.”
 UMG has similar ambitions for fan remixes. This year it announced licensing deals with Spotify and ElevenLabs, an AI audio startup, that would enable UMG’s material to be reworked by “superfans”. Sam Duboff, Spotify’s head of marketing, says there is demand. On some platforms, he reckons, unlicensed remixes and covers number 1bn a month; Spotify wants to regularise the market. Michael Nash of UMG says the company reckons 20-30% of streaming customers would pay up to twice the price of their current subscription for access to AI-enabled superfan products.
 A lot depends on how many leading performers opt in. Mr Nash hopes 1,000 UMG artists will. But so far UMG, WMG, Spotify and Suno have named no big stars who have signed up, suggesting that qualms related to artistic integrity remain high. And until top names agree to take part, it is hard to know how enthusiastic their fans will be.
 MIDiA’s Mr Mulligan says partnerships between record labels and makers of AI music have a defensive quality: the industry’s giants, whether labels or streaming platforms, want to reinforce the status quo. “They want to control AI, rather than have AI control them,” he says. But they might be bypassed

docs.title: Your wish is an AI agent's command—and that's a problem for the internet at large
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Your wish is an AI agent's command—and that's a problem for the internet at large
 Parmy Olson 4 min read 6 Oct 2026, 03:50 PM IST 
 Summary
 Artificial intelligence (AI) bots like OpenClaw, Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots are arguably very useful—and cute. But when trained to achieve goals by any means necessary, they could potentially wreak havoc. The world wide web had better watch out. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Earlier this year an Australian tech worker asked his OpenClaw artificial intelligence (AI) agent whether it could get him higher up on the waiting list for a popular gym class. It did exactly what he wanted, but with an unexpected twist: It found a flaw in the system and cancelled the booking of another person on the list. 
 AI’s next big magic trick is to start doing things for users across the web, with new tools like Muse from Meta and Dots from OpenAI working 24x7 to find online bargains, book restaurant tables or check emails. What’s troubling is how these increasingly capable and arguably useful tools are trained to find creative ways to meet their goals, which could lead to unintended consequences when unleashed on an internet full of poorly secured websites. 
 The Australian tech worker’s AI agent had found a loophole and exploited it without being told to. So what happens when millions of other people’s agents start competing for the cheapest flights or the best movie seats? In the best-case scenario, we will see a smooth and well-functioning network of bots that play by the rules to get the best outcomes for their humans. In the worst: a cyber security nightmare. 
 The web simply might not be ready. Security firm DataDome says 65% of the more than 20,000 websites it tested had systems for detecting or blocking AI agents, and that bot activity hitting login pages rose more than eightfold in the first half of 2026. 
 In some ways it is hard to imagine these new AI agents causing widespread trouble. They look too cute for a start. Muse has a cartoonish design reminiscent of a Labubu doll, while the vividly covered blobs that represent dots could be characters in a children’s TV show—perhaps part of an effort to ease general mistrust of Meta and OpenAI. 
 They work well too. Bloomberg ’s Dave Lee called Muse “the most impressive product Meta has released in years.” He said his agent, which he had christened Harold, had organized his calendar and scoured Facebook Marketplace for good deals. 
 Both Meta and OpenAI say they have strong guardrails in place to make sure their agents behave themselves. Muse is kept within an isolated virtual machine—essentially a private computer in Meta’s cloud—while a separate security system controls every request it makes on the internet, handling payments and making sure a human is consulted before any major task like buying something or sending a message. Dots is monitored in a similar way. 
 But even these safeguards don’t fix an underlying problem baked into today’s Generative AI models through training: a tendency to look for shortcuts, a phenomenon researchers call reward-hacking. This is also why chatbots are prone to flattery. The UK’s AI Security Institute noticed a rise in this kind of cheating behaviour in coding agents and chatbots late last year. 
 An inclination to please is what drove OpenAI’s agents to hack Hugging Face a few months ago. OpenAI agents also improperly meddled with the websites of dozens of other organizations this year, including the US Securities and Exchange Commission and Australia’s government-run healthcare scheme. Meta says one of its AI models too hacked another company of its own accord . 
 These cases happened while the models were being trained or tested, with safeguards deliberately lowered. But the bots’ actions still surprised their developers and researchers have noticed that even when they make their tests harder to game, agents keep trying to cheat. 
 There are signs that AI products will also hunt for loopholes in the wild, particularly in coding. In one instance, a software developer told his AI agent to clear out temporary files from a computer folder without using the ‘delete’ command. The agent then hid that instruction inside a testing tool and slipped past the filter to clear the files using the command it was told not to. 
 Now multiply that type of behaviour by million of agents as consumers explore using AI to optimize their lives and work. When Meta boss Mark Zuckerberg launched Muse last month, he said consumers deserved to have access to their own “personal superintelligence” and that the new agents would “make you money.” 
 Some aren’t doing that very well. When a consumer tech reviewer in Toronto named Matt J. Robb tried using Muse to sell a keyboard on Facebook Marketplace last month, the agent angered the buyer by saying Robb was at home to carry out the transaction, which wasn’t true. The agent had also made a low-ball offer. 
 On top of the risk of cheating, agents can also just make mistakes, and it will likely be end users who pay the price. Robb was left with a negative rating from his angry buyer. 
 However cuddly these new agents look, the systems behind them are trained to tick a box one way or another. They might do it a little too well. ©Bloomberg 
 The author is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist covering technology.

docs.title: The economics of group health distribution
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 The economics of group health distribution
 Kapil Mehta 4 min read 6 Oct 2026, 11:09 AM IST 
 Summary
 Irdai’s proposed distribution reforms need to account for the economics of group health insurance, where commissions are already low and intermediaries provide significant services to employers and employees. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Over the past few weeks, there has been considerable discussion around the Irdai consultation paper on distribution reforms. A central premise of the paper is that insurance commissions are too high and contribute to the difficulties policyholders face.
 Insurance is a diverse industry, and the challenges vary across segments. Retail health, motor and credit life insurance each merit their own analysis. I write about group health insurance for company employees, a segment I know well. It is a large, growing market in which intermediaries play a significant role. But here, commission is not the central issue.
 Before 2017, the commission allowed for brokers was 17.5% of premium. Subsequently, until 2023, the commission limit in employer-employee group health was reduced to 7.5%, with an additional reward on top. In 2023, specific product-level limits were done away with. Since then, commission for large and small companies has remained mostly unchanged, well under 7.5% for large companies and between 7.5% and 10% for smaller businesses. The only change was that commission and reward were merged.
 Thin economics
 Consider the economics of distributing group health insurance . For a company with 100 lives, the typical annual premium is about ₹ 6 lakh. Intermediaries will generally earn ₹ 45,000 as commission and incur costs of about ₹ 40,000, leaving a profit of ₹ 5,000, or about a 10% margin.
 What are these costs that intermediaries incur? A salesperson would have engaged with 10 potential clients to successfully close one. In each of those 10 engagements, the salesperson will suggest coverages, evaluate current benefits, benchmark quotes typically from five insurers and negotiate with insurers to get the best terms. Clients, even small ones, work with multiple intermediaries to drive prices down. There is a very effective price-lowering auction operating.
 After placement, a policy moves to servicing. Each year, there will be five to 10 engagement meetings with HR and employees explaining benefits. With 100 lives, there will be six to 10 claims a year that will be managed by the claims team, who will help at hospital discharge for cashless claims and with claim filing for reimbursements. Costs increase when insurers ask for original bills.
 Each time an employee joins or leaves, the intermediary must update the employee list, recalculate premiums and deliver health cards. Such endorsements happen about 12 to 15 times a year. Some insurers require a person to physically visit their office for endorsement.
 Technology adds costs through employee surveys, portals and apps. Finally, clients expect intermediaries to provide value-added services such as webinars, as on the recent World Heart Day, onsite activities, with Zumba a favourite, and health checkups, among other related services.
 If commission is capped at 2.5%, revenue will reduce to ₹ 15,000, resulting in a loss of ₹ 25,000 to the intermediary. This is unsustainable, and technology or cost-cutting cannot bridge this gap. All the activities I have described must be done for effective delivery, and removing an intermediary does not do away with the tasks.
 An outlier 
 The consultation paper reports that the maximum commission on group health insurance was 93% of premium. This is an outlier. Why did the insurer pay so much? No one can force them. Why did the client, for that matter, agree to this? Was it an affinity group where members bore the cost?
 This should be considered a market conduct issue rather than symptomatic of the industry. In employer-employee group insurance, I have consistently found insurers stingy, unwilling to part with a single extra rupee of commission.
 Intermediaries have limited room to negotiate. Virtually every group health client works with multiple intermediaries to discover price floors. If one intermediary were to price the insurance high for more commission, another would win the account with better terms. This keeps the system fair.
 Look at underwriting
 Insurers do lose money on group health. But this is because of their underwriting practices rather than commission.
 Consider that public sector insurers, which pay the lowest commissions, have the highest claim ratio in group health, at 104% in FY25, as per Irdai’s annual report. Insurers must strengthen their underwriting discipline. They should walk away from competitive situations that require them to quote low or pay excess commission.
 When the final regulations are notified, the regulator could factor in the cost of providing service. It should consider significantly higher rates for smaller companies and MSMEs .
 Improving policyholder outcomes is singularly important. This is essential for intermediaries too if we are to retain clients and scale up.
 The solutions require a segment-wise assessment of issues and careful consideration of unintended consequences, rather than a broad-brush approach.
 Kapil Mehta, co-founder, SecureNow Insurance Broker.

docs.title: Resistance to data centres is arising in India too: It’s time for policy to address people’s concerns
docs.text:
Opinion 
 Resistance to data centres is arising in India too: It’s time for policy to address people’s concerns
 Rahul Matthan 5 min read 6 Oct 2026, 04:00 PM IST 
 Summary
 Data centres needn’t guzzle as much water and power as protestors say. Nor need they be all that noisy. But people who live in proximity of data-centre sites do have worries we can’t dismiss. The government should take these into account, lest they get in the way of plans. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 This July, several hundred residents of Thane formed a human chain outside a 53-acre plot in Balkum that had been earmarked for a hyperscale data centre. They were agitating against the noise and heat it would generate, and the water it would consume in a city that is already struggling to supply its residents. This, as far as I can tell, was the first time Indians have taken to the streets against a data centre. It will not be the last. 
 The arguments they were making are not new. Claims that each question we put to ChatGPT consumes half a litre of water and uses 10 times the electricity of a Google search have been around since 2023. 
 But the soundness of these allegations have been questioned. The figures, it is said, come from outdated publications that misrepresent current facts. In August last year, Google stated that a median text prompt to Gemini consumes 0.24 watt-hours of electricity and 0.26 millilitres (about five drops) of water. If this is correct, then each prompt costs roughly what a Google search does—far less than what is alleged. 
 But Google’s figure is a median for text and conveniently ignores the fact that reasoning models consume a hundred times and video generators about 4,000 times that figure for a 5-second clip. 
 What is much harder to defend is the noise pollution caused by the incessant whine of fans that are needed to keep servers cool. Because of its steady, low frequency, it carries in a way that noise pollution caused by traffic does not. That said, a well-built data centre can keep the sound to between 45 and 65 decibels at its fence, which is quieter than a highway. 
 The other concerns are also less alarming than they appear to be at first glance. Data centres used about 1.5% of the world’s electricity in 2024 and produced 0.5% of its emissions from fuel combustion. This is about a fifth of the energy we consume for air-conditioning and the International Energy Agency expects them to account for less than a tenth of additional demand projected till 2030. 
 The Council on Energy, Environment and Water puts Indian data centres at two or three hundredths of a per cent of our water demand. 
 None of this is to suggest that protestors in Thane are wrong to worry. The environmental cost of AI should not be calculated on a per-prompt basis, but must instead be evaluated in terms of where each data centre is built, what powers it, and who it is going to affect because they live next door to it. In Ireland, since hyperscalers were allowed to cluster around Dublin, 23% of its electricity now goes to data centres. 
 Two-thirds of the data centres built in the US since 2022 sit in places already short of water. By that reckoning, India is also building them in exactly the wrong places. Google’s $15 billion AI hub in Visakhapatnam is coming up in a district with the lowest groundwater in Andhra Pradesh, while Mumbai, which accounts for over half of our installed data centre capacity, had to ration water this summer. 
 The draft National Data Centre Policy that India’s ministry of electronics and information technology (IT) circulated last year ties its incentives to power-usage effectiveness (the ratio of the electricity a facility draws to what its servers actually use). 
 However, it does not appear to have addressed issues about water, siting or noise. Since the cheapest route to power-usage effectiveness is evaporative cooling, we may find ourselves trading electricity efficiency for chronic water shortages. 
 Last year, I argued in this column that we should run the same playbook that built our IT industry to succeed at AI. But that is only half of what we need to do. The other half has to do with addressing the concerns of Balkum’s residents. 
 What needs to be done is not difficult. Wherever measures like this have been demanded, they have eventually been taken. When a Uruguayan court forced Google to disclose that its Canelones data centre would draw 7.6 million litres of drinking water a day, the public reaction was enough to get the company to redesign it to run on air-cooled chillers. 
 Microsoft’s Hyderabad data centre runs a closed loop that consumes almost no water for cooling. In Chandler, Arizona, the noise produced by a data centre can never exceed the ambient level of the baseline recorded prior to construction. Karnataka’s new policy requires data centres to report their water use every year, and Maharashtra has commissioned standards for siting, water and noise. 
 Our national policy must address these concerns head on. Every data centre should be obliged to report both its water-usage and power-usage effectiveness. Every new site should pass a test that weighs the water stress of the basin it draws from and the homes that depend on the same water. 
 The noise it emits while operating at peak load should never exceed the baseline measured before construction. None of this will slow the industry down. These are all measures that have been adopted elsewhere and the technology exists to make it feasible. 
 Stories about the amount of water AI consumes will outlive our attempts to correct the narrative—because the myth is far more vivid than reality. But all that residents of Balkum really want is the assurance that the facility that’s being built would not impose an impossible burden on those who have to live with it. These are concerns that our data centre policy c

docs.title: Inside Bessent’s treasury: tension, turnover and unmet economic goals
docs.text:
Global 
 Inside Bessent’s treasury: tension, turnover and unmet economic goals
 Brian Schwartz , Josh Dawsey , Philip Wegmann , Gregory Zuckerman , The Wall Street Journal 15 min read 7 Oct 2026, 06:52 AM IST 
 Summary
 Ahead of midterms that could turn on high prices and borrowing costs, the secretary dresses down officials. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 WASHINGTON—Scott Bessent was fuming.
 President Trump had just asked his Treasury secretary to investigate allegations of fraud in Minnesota’s Somali community—and Bessent thought one of his top deputies was dragging his feet.
 During a January meeting at the Treasury Department, Bessent confronted John Hurley, the agency’s undersecretary for terrorism and financial intelligence, yelling at him in front of aides and unleashing profanities. Bessent shouted so loudly that staff working nearby could hear him, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.
 Weeks later, Bessent discussed with aides the idea of finding Hurley, who had been confirmed by the Senate for his position, a job outside the department, the people said. Hurley left to be U.S. ambassador to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development. It was one of a string of high-level departures in the top ranks of the department at a moment when the Treasury secretary was staring down the biggest challenges of his career.
 Bessent’s behavior was a factor—and sometimes the most-important one—in the departure of multiple key officials, people familiar with the matter said.
 Since he became Treasury secretary in early 2025, Bessent has dressed down senior advisers and junior staffers alike over issues large and small, according to more than a dozen current and former Treasury officials.
 But Trump has only pulled Bessent closer, empowering him to solve stubborn problems in the economy, including higher borrowing costs, intractable inflation pushed up by gas prices and government debt that is piling up quickly. At the same time, Bessent has been tasked with ending the war in Iran with a sweeping sanctions plan.
 A senior administration official who worked with Bessent said the president’s entire economic policy agenda is on the Treasury secretary’s shoulders. “Scott cannot fail,” the official said.
 His backers say his hard-charging style gets results. But 20 months into his tenure at the department, Bessent is facing skepticism on Wall Street and an economy that could wreck Republican chances in November’s midterm elections.
 Bessent advised Trump to pursue a “3-3-3” policy: cutting the budget deficit to 3% of gross domestic product by 2028, spurring GDP growth of 3% and producing an additional three million barrels of oil a day. But growth has been around 2%, and oil production has increased less than a million barrels a day since Trump took office. The budget deficit is now over 6% of GDP, according to the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget. U.S. debt overall recently topped $40 trillion.
 A deepening selloff in U.S. government bonds has driven the yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury note to highs last seen more than two decades ago, despite a stepped-up buyback program Bessent set into motion to contain the increase. The result is higher borrowing costs for Americans, a perilous trend for Republicans.
 The Iran war, meanwhile, has no clear end in sight, although there are signs the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports and economic squeeze engineered by the Trump administration is making the regime more desperate for a way out. But the president recently rejected Iran’s offer for a deal and has also told aides he expects another U.S. bombing campaign against Iran after the midterms.

He has dismissed his critics as “Bloomberg terminal bros,” referring to those on Wall Street questioning his moves, and quipped in a recent interview, “I am the house now,” citing the insights he has gained as Treasury secretary. “You can bet against me if you want.”

 And his temper has flared. He has shouted at staff for not moving fast enough to implement his ideas and for failing to combat unfavorable media coverage, some of the officials said. Last year, Bessent got so angry about the way his daily briefing book was organized that he picked up the binder full of papers and threw it at a wall, people familiar with the matter said.
 Bessent denied the account to The Wall Street Journal.

Nifty may move towards 22,900, says MOFSL; shares 3 stock ideas
 Nifty has to hold above the 22,700 zones for an upside move towards 22,900, then 23,000 zones, while support can be seen at 22,600.
 Nifty may move towards 22,900, says MOFSL; shares 3 stock ideas
 Chandan Taparia Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 07 2026 | 7:46 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Disclaimer: This article is written by Chandan Taparia, head, derivatives & technicals, wealth management, Motilal Oswal Financial Services. Views expressed are his own. Readers' discretion is advised. 
 Nifty index opened positive and remained in a sideways to positive trend throughout the session and moved up by more than 200 points. The index closed near its upper band and has started to make higher highs – higher lows from the last two sessions. It formed a bullish candle on the daily frame, indicating support-based buying at lower levels. Now it has to hold above the 22,700 zones for an upside move towards 22,900, then 23,000 zones, while support can be seen at 22,600 then 22,500 zones.

Mutual funds log 5% AUM growth in Q2 despite equity market volatility
 Mutual fund houses' average quarterly assets under management rose to ₹87.2 trillion in Q2FY27 from ₹83.1 trillion in Q1, supported by strong inflows across categories
 According to experts, while the debt fund inflows were led by short-term institutional investments, the active equity fund inflows were driven by systematic investment plan (SIP) inflows
 Abhishek Kumar 2 min read Last Updated : Oct 07 2026 | 7:49 AM IST
 Listen to This Article
 Mutual funds (MFs) logged nearly 5 per cent growth in average quarterly assets under management (QAAUM) in the second quarter (Q2) of 2026-27 (FY27) despite the equity market turbulence. Fund houses had a QAAUM of ₹87.2 trillion in Q2, up from ₹83.1 trillion in Q1. 
 The growth was highest in three quarters, shows data released by the Association of Mutual Funds in India (Amfi).
 The growth was supported by strong inflows across categories in a quarter where there were mark-to-market losses in equity schemes owing to market correction, especially in the largecap segment. Some of the debt schemes also witnessed correction.
 In the first two months (July and August) of Q2, investors poured a net ₹54,000 crore into active equity schemes. Overall, across categories, the net inflows stood at ₹2.8 trillion during the two-month period. Debt funds garnered the most of the inflows.

Soft Q2 order inflows, commodity inflation weigh on capital goods firms
 Order inflows for major capital goods firms excluding L&T may fall 10 per cent Y-o-Y in Q2FY27, while higher commodity prices are likely to squeeze margins
 premium 
 Representative image for capital goods
 Devangshu Datta New Delhi 4 min read Last Updated : Oct 06 2026 | 11:52 PM IST
 Listen to This Article
 The cumulative order inflows of major capital goods companies in Q2FY27 (excluding Larsen & Toubro or L&T) may be worth ₹35,000 crore, down by around 10 per cent year-on-year (Y-o-Y).
 L&T announced inflows of ₹1 trillion in Q2FY27, which included three orders of over ₹15,000 crore in hydrocarbons from West Asia, and two orders of over ₹10,000 crore from Nvidia and NTPC. 
 However, defence order inflows were up 19 per cent Y-o-Y at ₹8,600 crore, if those orders are adjusted for the base effect of a Light Combat Aircraft (LCA) order to Hindustan Aeronautics Limited (HAL) for 97 aircraft worth ₹62,300 crore in Q2FY26. 
 The defence inflows saw delays in finalisation of quick reaction surface-to-air missiles (QRSAM), Project-75I (P75I), and next generation corvettes (NGCs).
 Given the large outstanding order books, and assuming steady execution, there’s good revenue visibility for the next several quarters. But margin pressures must have been significant, given high commodity prices. Earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (Ebitda) margins are almost guaranteed to compress in Q2 and beyond, and export orders to West Asia may see delays.
 Apart from defence, there were big orders in power transmission and distribution (T&D), with the segment’s order book up 120 per cent Y-o-Y to ₹13,700 crore. During Q2FY27, order inflows were contributed by hydrocarbons, power transmission, real estate, metro and rail. There seems to be some revival in private capex which is contributing to orders from manufacturing, oil and gas, data centres, and renewables.
 Given the known capacity for execution, sales of electrical majors like ABB India, Siemens and Thermax may all have risen by mid-teens Y-o-Y.
 Cummins’ sales may also grow by around 14 per cent. Among other players, BEML’s sales may rise by over 20 per cent due to rail and metro orders. Jyoti CNC automation’s sales may rise 20 per cent and KEC International’s sales may grow by high-single-digits, again with T&D orders dominating the mix.
 Solar equipment manufacturers will have seen steady execution and possible rise in volumes. Waaree Energies and Premier Energies should have both seen revenue growth of 25 per cent or better Y-o-Y.
 Power transmission equipment has seen stable inflows and the pipeline is witnessing momentum.
 CG Power and Hitachi Energy should have mid-teens growth or better in order inflows.
 Some analysts are very bullish about these companies. GE Vernova may see a fall in orders, or a rise, depending on whether a big HVDC order ($1.5 billion) for the Barmer-South Kalamb project is booked in Q2FY27 or in Q3FY27.
 Defence sales are known to be lumpy and subject to delays. But Bharat Dynamics’ sales may rise 25 per cent Y-o-Y. While Garden Reach Shipbuilders revenue may rise 15 per cent Y-o-Y and Bharat Electronics’ sales could be up by early teens or low double-digits. And, HAL’s revenue may rise by mid-teens.
 HAL will receive 12 additional engines from GE by December 2026. According to the Ministry of Defence, GE has supplied 10 engines to HAL and will supply 4 engines each month from October to December.
 Reportedly, HAL has 27 Tejas Mk1A airframes ready and expects to deliver one squadron of Tejas Mk1A by 2026, which is much better than earlier estimates.
 The outlier on the growth front in the defence segment is expected to be Zen Technologies’ which could see a surge of 40-50 per cent in revenues if execution improves. Solar Industries’ revenue could also rise by 40 per cent.
 L&T may see high-single-digit growth in its core business. International execution was cautious due to the Iran conflict. However, there was a likely quarter-on-quarter (Q-o-Q) acceleration in core execution and H2FY27 may see further acceleration. The non-core business for L&T may see mid-teens sales growth. Cummins may see a slowdown in exports due to geopolitical tensions.
 Among key commodities, zinc, copper, aluminium and pig iron all saw double-digit inflation Q-o-Q in Q2FY27. This would hurt gross margins but some of it may have been offset by hikes.
 Margin compression in Q2FY27 could be particularly high for solar manufacturers.
 Ongoing projects with fixed price contracts without pass-through clauses will also be badly affected.
 Margin trends will be crucial, going forward, since pricing power may not be strong enough to fully offset raw material inflation.

docs.title: Nomura cuts Nifty target to 24,000 as US yields rise: Why IT, banks, auto are safe bets
docs.text: Nomura has cut its March 2027 target for the Nifty 50 to 24,000, lowering its one-year forward valuation multiple to 17 times from 18.5 times earlier as global bond yields rise. At the same time, the brokerage remains positive on financials, information technology services, auto ancillaries, engineering and manufacturing, capital goods and pharmaceuticals, while taking a cautious view on consumption. The new Nifty 50 target is based on FY28 earnings per share of 1,410 and a 17-times forward earnings multiple. Nomura's calculation gives a target of 23,970 before rounding, implying a 7% potential return based on the level cited on October 1, 2026. Why Nomura sees the latest market correction differently Nomura stated that the latest decline in Indian equities has been driven by more than crude oil and geopolitical tensions. The brokerage compares the August-September correction with the February-March sell-off and points to a different pattern across sectors. ALSO READFrom 7.1% to 15.3%: HDFC Bank’s loan growth comeback is hard to ignore During the first phase, oil-sensitive and domestic-cycle segments such as oil marketing companies, banks, real estate and autos bore the brunt of the decline. In the second phase, information technology services fell the most, while non-banking finance companies and consumer staples also lagged despite solid first-quarter FY27 earnings. According to Nomura, "The correction, in our view, reflects deeper structural concerns. The correction reflects growing apprehension around long-term growth, rooted in geopolitical realignment and technological disruption and their potential adverse implications for India. Unlike in the first leg of the correction, the AI investment narrative remained firmly intact during the second, reinforcing the relative attractiveness of the US market." The brokerage also pointed to policy and regulatory risks in areas such as insurance and hospitals, adding to the pressure on some segments. ALSO READBPCL, HPCL, IOC in focus: Morgan Stanley sees a 3-year refining upswing Higher US yields are changing the valuation equation Global bond yields have become another important factor in Nomura's market assessment. US 10-year and 30-year Treasury yields have risen 74 basis points and 65 basis points, respectively, over three months, moving above 5%. The India-US 10-year yield differential has narrowed to 190 basis points, its lowest level in 22 years. Foreign institutional investors have also stepped up selling. Nomura put financial-year-to-date net outflows from Indian equities at $12.5 billion, with selling intensifying in September after relative stability during July and August. Healthcare was the only sector to escape the selling, according to the brokerage. Nomura wrote, "The yield spread between India and the US has declined even further. For 10-year treasury, the difference between India and the US is at 190bp, the lowest in 22 years. The rise in yields in developed markets is driven by strong growth and credit demand, rather than expectations of any long-term inflationary pressures." Nomura cuts Nifty March target to 24,000 Nomura has reduced its target multiple for the Nifty 50 to 17 times one-year forward earnings from 18.5 times earlier. Its March 2027 target stands at 24,000, based on FY28 earnings per share of 1,410. The brokerage's calculation produces a target of 23,970 before rounding, while its FY26-FY28 earnings-per-share compound annual growth rate is 6.9%. The report puts the potential return at 7% based on the Nifty level as of October 1, 2026. Nomura said, "We reduce our target multiple to 17.0x 1-year forward from 18.5x previously, and assign a March 2027 target of Rs 24,000 for the Nifty50. The reduction in target multiple factors in higher yields. We do not assume structural headwinds from geopolitics and technological changes to have long-term impact on growth." The lower multiple is therefore primarily linked to the higher yield environment rather than an assumption that India's longer-term growth prospects have permanently weakened. Valuations have fallen, but reset is uneven The Nifty 50 is trading at 16.9 times one-year forward earnings, marginally below its 17-22 times post-pandemic range and slightly below its pre-pandemic average. Nomura's assessment becomes more divided further down the market-cap spectrum. The Nifty Midcap index trades at 22.9 times one-year forward earnings against a post-pandemic average of 29.4 times. The Nifty Smallcap index, however, trades at 23.7 times, above its post-pandemic average of 22.9 times. Its 39.3% premium over the Nifty 50 is the highest in more than a decade. Nomura wrote, "The mid caps and the small caps in particular have been relatively more resilient. The segment represents companies with low base, that can adapt to changing dynamics quickly and record much stronger growth vs large caps. Nifty mid caps trade at 22.9x against a post-pandemic average of 29.4x, a meaningful reset." The brokerage also notes that financials, information technology and consumption now trade below pre-pandemic multiples, while auto ancillaries, pharmaceuticals, real estate and defence/capital goods continue to trade at a premium. docs.title: Nomura initiates coverage on this optical cable play: Datacentre capex to fuel 35% rally?
docs.text: The optical fibre cable (OFC) industry is at a multi-year super cycle, driven by strong datacentre capital expenditure tailwinds, and one company, Sterlite Technologies, is in the middle of it all. The company is well poised to benefit from the robust OFC demand due to its integrated capacity. Global brokerage Nomura has initiated coverage on the stock with a ‘Buy’ rating and has set a target price of Rs 1,350 apiece. This implies a nearly 35% upside from the stock’s closing price on Monday at Rs 1,001.25 apiece. Nomura has valued Sterlite Tech at 30 times December 2028 earnings per share. “Our target multiple is at 20% discount to the long-term average one-year forward P/E ratio of Polycab and KEI…,” the brokerage said. Nomura said the demand cycle for OFC is expected to persist beyond 2030. It sees a 14% growth in OFC demand on a compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) basis over 2025-2030 in North America and Europe, the key markets for Sterlite Tech. “However, constrained supply due to limited glass preform capacity, raw material bottlenecks, and limited ex-China capacity have created a persistent deficit, forcing hyperscalers into multi-year supply agreements and opening opportunities for players such as STL,” it said. ALSO READ2 Indian stocks up 205-690% as America builds more data centres and pipelines Nomura on Sterlite Tech: Integrated facility Sterlite Tech’s integrated manufacturing capability positions it to capture market share as its non-integrated peers face “preform supply bottleneck”. The company has already secured major hyperscaler contracts and has an extensive array of data centre offerings. “The company has a 9% share in the ex-China global OFC market (1Q1FY27) and its DC (data centre) market share, (low-single digits currently) can increase towards high single-digits, in our view, due to its superior product portfolio, established relation with hyperscalers and extensive industry experience,” Nomura said. Nomura on Sterlite Tech: Earnings outlook The company plans to invest Rs 3,000 crore over the next three years to expand capacity by 50%, supported by strong demand visibility. Its revenue from data centres is expected to rise to nearly 40% of total revenue by FY29 from 1% in FY26, Nomura said, adding that optical connectivity is also expected to scale rapidly. This is expected to drive earnings before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortisation (EBITDA) margin to 24% from 12%, as orders from data centres fetch high margins. Nomura expects Sterlite Tech’s revenue to grow by 50% on a CAGR basis over FY26 to FY29 and EBITDA to grow by 89% CAGR over the same period. ALSO READJefferies initiates coverage on Dhoot Transmission: Here’s why it sees 14% upside Nomura on Sterlite Tech: Key risks The brokerage said a slowing capital expenditure towards artificial intelligence led data centres and faster than expected commissioning of industry capacity are the key risks to its outlook for Sterlite Tech. Nomura also believes weaker than expected optical infrastructure and execution and cash outgo due to legal claims pose significant risks. Nomura on Sterlite Tech: Well poised to capture OFC demand The brokerage remains bullish on the stock, projecting a 35% upside. Sterlite Tech remains well poised to benefit from the surge in demand and capital spends on data centres, which are likely to remain till 2030. docs.title: Motilal Oswal initiates coverage on Truenat maker Molbio; sees 19% upside
docs.text: Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd. has initiated coverage on Molbio Diagnostics Ltd. with a ‘Buy’ rating and a target price of Rs 1,800, seeing room for the company to build a broader diagnostics franchise beyond its established tuberculosis testing business. The brokerage expects Molbio’s Truenat platform, recurring test-kit sales, new assays such as HPV, international expansion and newer businesses in imaging and digital pathology to support strong earnings growth over the next three years. Motilal Oswal’s target price implies a potential upside of about 19%. The brokerage has based its valuation on a 45-times multiple of 12-month forward earnings, a 20% premium to the sector multiple of 36 times. Why Motilal Oswal initiated coverage on Molbio The investment case centres on Molbio’s Truenat platform, a portable, battery-operated polymerase chain reaction system designed for point-of-care molecular testing. The platform can deliver results in about 60 minutes and requires less infrastructure than conventional centralised PCR testing. Molbio had more than 12,500 Truenat devices deployed across more than 90 countries as of March 2026, with 43 assays covering 30 diseases. Motilal Oswal Financial Services Ltd. said the company is also moving beyond molecular diagnostics through Prognosys in imaging and OptraSCAN in digital pathology. ALSO READGoldman Sachs rates 2 PSU banks ‘Sell’ despite credit growth – Here’s why The brokerage’s broader thesis is that Molbio Diagnostics Ltd. is moving from selling diagnostic devices to building a recurring consumables-led business around its installed base. Motilal Oswal analysts Tushar Manudhane, Vipul Mehta, Eshita Jain and Khyati Sonthalia said, "We believe Molbio is well positioned to capture the opportunity in decentralized molecular diagnostics via its integrated Truenat ecosystem, combining proprietary molecular diagnostic devices with a recurring test-kit franchise. The expanding installed base, widening assay menu and global scale-up provide multiple levers for sustainable growth, while increasing utilization should drive operating leverage." Truenat consumables lead growth as test-kit sales outpace equipment ALSO READFrom 7.1% to 15.3%: HDFC Bank’s loan growth comeback is hard to ignore Truenat contributed about 90% of Molbio’s revenue in FY26, making the platform the central part of the brokerage’s earnings case. Motilal Oswal expects Truenat revenue to grow at about 16% annually between FY26 and FY29, supported by more devices, higher utilisation of the existing installed base and additional assays. The business model is increasingly weighted towards test kits rather than equipment. Between FY23 and FY26, Truenat device sales grew at an 18% compound annual growth rate, while test-kit sales grew at 84%. TB test kits accounted for 74% of consumables revenue in FY26. The installed base also leaves room for higher utilisation. Truenat is deployed across about 8,000-9,000 diagnostic centres in India, while a significant number of TB diagnostic centres continue to rely on microscopy-based testing. Motilal Oswal expects conversion from microscopy to molecular testing to support further device placements and recurring test-kit consumption. Cervical cancer screening: How HPV assays could fuel next demand surge TB remains the anchor application for Truenat, but Motilal Oswal sees HPV testing as an important opportunity to increase utilisation of the existing installed base. The brokerage noted that Molbio’s HPV assay underwent validation led by AIIMS in collaboration with international agencies, including the World Health Organization and Gates Foundation. The report said the test was the only Indian assay among multiple indigenous HPV DNA tests evaluated to meet the prescribed international criteria, after which a recommendation was made to the government for rollout under the national programme. The report also said a government health technology assessment found Truenat’s HPV test cost-effective at the offered price for screening women aged 30-45. A potential national screening programme could therefore provide another recurring source of test-kit demand. Motilal Oswal also sees a potential international opportunity if the HPV assay receives World Health Organization prequalification, which could allow Molbio to participate in international procurement programmes and expand into emerging markets pursuing cervical cancer screening. Molbio’s earnings could accelerate as utilisation improves Motilal Oswal expects the combination of higher test-kit consumption, installed-base expansion and international sales to support a 23% revenue compound annual growth rate between FY26 and FY29. The brokerage expects operating leverage to push EBITDA growth faster than revenue, while adjusted profit after tax is projected to rise at a 50% compound annual growth rate over the same period. docs.title: Goldman Sachs rates 2 PSU banks ‘Sell’ despite credit growth – Here’s why
docs.text: Goldman Sachs has taken a fresh look at India’s public sector banks after seven lenders reported their second-quarter business updates, with credit growth improving but still trailing the broader banking system. The brokerage expects the next phase to depend not just on loan growth, but also on deposit mobilisation, funding conditions and the ability of banks to sustain earnings as credit costs normalise. Goldman Sachs has retained its ‘Sell’ ratings on Bank of Baroda and Punjab National Bank, even as both lenders reported year-on-year improvement in parts of their balance sheets. The brokerage has a 12-month target price of Rs 245 for Bank of Baroda and Rs 103 for Punjab National Bank. Based on the prices cited in the report, that implies about 6% upside for Bank of Baroda and about 6% downside for Punjab National Bank. PSU banks are growing, but banking system is moving faster Seven public sector banks had reported their balance sheet updates when Goldman Sachs published its 5 October report. The group comprises Bank of Baroda, Punjab National Bank, Canara Bank, Union Bank of India, Bank of India, Indian Bank and UCO Bank. Together, these lenders account for about 65% of public sector bank credit, while State Bank of India is excluded because it does not report initial business updates. Goldman Sachs said aggregate domestic credit growth for these seven banks reached about 16% year-on-year in the second quarter of FY27, compared with 15% in the previous quarter. That represents a 60-basis-point acceleration, but the broader banking system recorded a much sharper improvement, with system credit growth reaching 18% as of September 15. ALSO READFrom 7.1% to 15.3%: HDFC Bank’s loan growth comeback is hard to ignore The same pattern was visible in deposits. Aggregate domestic deposit growth for the seven banks improved from about 10% year-on-year in the previous quarter to around 13% in the second quarter, but remained below system deposit growth of 17%. Goldman Sachs analysts stated that "With LCRs now largely converged between private and PSU banks, the liquidity advantage enjoyed by state-owned banks over the past few years has diminished. At the same time, stronger FCNR(B) deposit mobilisation has improved funding availability for private banks." Bank of Baroda gets support from retail lending, deposits Bank of Baroda’s domestic advances grew 13.5% year-on-year in the second quarter of FY27, while domestic deposits increased 17%. The bank’s retail advances remained the main source of loan growth, rising 18.7% year-on-year. Goldman Sachs noted that the retail book continued to hold up even as non-retail loan growth moderated. Its assessment was that domestic advances had grown 14% year-on-year, compared with 16% in the previous quarter, while deposits grew 17%, broadly matching system deposit growth. The brokerage said, "Loan growth continued to be driven by retail advances, which remained resilient at 19% YoY, broadly in line with recent quarters. In contrast, non-retail loan growth slowed meaningfully, declining from 15% YoY to 12% last qtr." Bank of Baroda’s domestic retail advances accounted for 27.3% of domestic advances in the second quarter, compared with 26.9% in the previous quarter. Domestic deposits rose 7.7% sequentially, taking the domestic credit-to-deposit ratio down to about 80% from 83% in the first quarter. The deposit performance is also important in the context of funding availability. Goldman Sachs said the sharp acceleration in deposit growth was partly helped by FCNR(B) deposit inflows, citing media reports of about US$8 billion, or roughly Rs 76,000 crore. ALSO READDLF to Godrej, Prestige: Morgan Stanley picks 3 realty stocks driving Rs 1.31 lk cr pre-sales Punjab National Bank sees credit growth pick up Punjab National Bank reported domestic credit growth of 12.6% year-on-year in the second quarter of FY27, up from 12.0% in the previous quarter. Deposit growth stood at 9.4%, keeping the lender below the pace seen at Bank of Baroda and the broader banking system. Goldman Sachs said PNB’s credit growth accelerated by 100 basis points from the previous quarter, while deposit growth remained broadly stable at 9%. The improvement pushed the bank’s credit-to-deposit ratio up by 150 basis points to 74%, marking the first meaningful acceleration after two quarters of broadly flat movement. The combination of faster credit growth and slower deposit growth means the bank is deploying a larger portion of its funding base towards loans. That will make the pace and quality of deposit mobilisation an important part of the earnings discussion as the bank moves into the second half of FY27. How the 7 PSU banks compare: Goldman view The business updates show a wide range of growth rates across the public sector banking group. UCO Bank recorded the fastest domestic credit growth at 26% year-on-year, followed by Bank of India at 17.7%, Union Bank of India at 17.4% and Canara Bank at 16.8%. Indian Bank grew 16.6%, while Bank of Baroda and Punjab National Bank were at 13.5% and 12.6%, respectively. docs.title: 7 wealth lessons from Sunil Gavaskar: How he turned 34 Test centuries into a ₹257 crore legacy
docs.text: Picture a hospital ward in Bombay, July 1949. A young man has just come to see his newborn nephew and noticed a small hole near the top of the baby's left ear. The next day he comes back, and the baby in the crib has no hole. Somebody has swapped the babies. The family goes looking, and the right child is eventually found asleep beside a fisherwoman. That baby was Sunil Gavaskar. Years later he would joke that his habit of poking at balls outside off stump came from that brief stint on the fishing side of life. I have known that story for a long time, but I never thought much about it. For most of my life I filed Gavaskar under "great opener, scored mountains of runs, wore a cap instead of a helmet against the fastest bowlers alive." Then I started reading about how he handled money, and the picture flipped. The man wasn't only a batsman with good sense. He was a businessman who happened to be very good at cricket, and every big decision in his career looks different once you see it that way. Most sportspeople retire and then panic. Twenty years of cover drives, and nobody ever taught them to read a contract. Gavaskar built a fortune often estimated around 250 crore rupees, and I wanted to understand how. These are the seven things I took from it. ALSO READHow Sunil Gavaskar turned 34 Test centuries into a multi-generational fortune 1. Treat your craft like a profession from day one Gavaskar grew up in a middle-class Marathi family in Bombay. His uncle Madhav Mantri had played Tests for India. His father worked in business. Nobody in that house treated cricket as a pastime. It was a job you trained for, the way other families trained a son for the accounts office. His routine at St Xavier's shows it. Three hours of practice before school, three more after. He was named India's best schoolboy cricketer in 1966, at a time when the best players in Bombay mostly got jobs at firms like Tata and ACC and played for company teams on weekends. Cricket didn't make you rich yet. It made you employable. He later boiled it down to what he called the three Ds: dedication, determination, discipline. It sounds like something from a school poster, but he actually lived on that schedule for years. I think the early seriousness is the reason the later money didn't ruin him. ALSO READFrom Payyoli Beach to Parliament: How India’s Golden Girl outran her era 2. Put a price on your wicket After scoring a double century in a school match, teenage Sunil got carried away and holed out trying to hit a six. Mantri was furious. His message was simple: put a price on your wicket. Never hand it over cheaply. That sentence turned into a whole way of batting. Gavaskar finished with 10,122 Test runs at an average of 51.12, and he was the first man past 10,000. Bowlers had to work for every one of those runs. It turned into a business habit too. Ad man Prahlad Kakkar has described Gavaskar as the first Indian cricketer to push up what endorsements were worth. Before him, players said yes to whatever number a company named. After him, they started asking what they were actually worth. I like that a lesson about not giving away a wicket ended up changing how a whole generation of cricketers negotiated. 3. Be ready before the chance shows up In 1971 Gavaskar went to the West Indies as a newcomer. A nail infection kept him out of the first Test. In the four he did play, he made 774 runs at 154.8, which is still a record for a debut series. India won, and it was their first series win in the Caribbean. Think about who he was facing. The West Indies attack was getting scarier by the year, and he played it with no helmet, relying on a technique so tidy that the dangerous stuff looked routine. That series gave him his brand. The Little Master, the man you couldn't blast out, the opener who made you earn him. Later in life, companies bought into exactly that picture: patient, careful, not reckless. Everyone talks about his luck on that tour. I don't buy it. He'd spent years on those three-hour sessions. The chance showed up and he was already standing there with his pads on. 4. Chase the session, not the target At The Oval in 1979, India needed 438 to win the final innings of the fourth Test. Nobody had ever made that many in a fourth innings and won. Gavaskar opened and scored 221 over more than eight hours. He began cautiously, then moved up through the gears as the game demanded it. India ended nine runs short, and people still bring that innings up. I can't know what was in his head out there, but the shape of the innings tells a story. When a number is too big to look at, you stop looking at it. You play the next session, then the next hour, then the next over. You deal with what's in front of you and let the total take care of itself. I have borrowed that for my own work more than once. A huge project becomes manageable when you cut it into overs. Gavaskar did the same thing in negotiations, by most accounts: go slowly, learn the pitch, and don't stake everything on one swing. 5. If you don't know your price, somebody else will pick one In October 1985, two years before his last Test, Gavaskar co-founded the Professional Management Group with ad executive Sumedh Shah. It was India's first dedicated sports marketing company. The way it started is my favourite part of this whole story. Shah asked Gavaskar what he charged for an endorsement. Gavaskar had to admit he didn't know. Shah said that was the problem with Indian sport in a sentence: athletes who couldn't name their own value would always be underpaid. PMG's first big project flopped. They brought a Swedish Davis Cup squad over, with Mats Wilander, then world number one, in the team. Indian advertisers weren't interested. They kept asking whether John McEnroe was coming. The event lost money, but it taught them something blunt about the market. In India, "sports marketing" meant cricket, and everything else came second. So they adjusted. In 1986 they started sponsored sy

docs.title: Stocks to watch on Oct 7: Titan, Mphasis, JSW Cement, banks in focus ahead of RBI policy
docs.text: Every trading day starts with the same quiet question - what will everyone be talking about by 9:15 AM? For October 7, the answer might be a jeweller, a tech firm, a cement maker and an entire banking sector and rate sensitives - all waiting for one announcement. Before looking at the outlook for October 7, a quick look at how markets fared on October 6. The Sensex closed at 73,067.81, up 685.34 points (0.95%), and the Nifty finished at 22,776.10, gaining 220.35 points (0.98%). The Nifty even picked up another 58 points during the closing auction session. Vinod Nair of Geojit Investments said, "Crude oil prices slipped below the $100 mark after a large G7 stockpile release and alternative supply measures helped offset disruptions to vessel movements through the Strait of Hormuz." ALSO READFrom 7.1% to 15.3%: HDFC Bank’s loan growth comeback is hard to ignore He added that this, along with strong Q2 updates from financials and retail, "improved investors' sentiment and supported a rebound from the oversold levels." Here is a look at the stocks that are likely to remain in focus on October 7 trading session - Titan The Q2FY27 earnings season has begun, while companies are also announcing their Q2 business updates. Titan reported 25% year-on-year growth across its consumer businesses in Q2 FY27. The company added 78 net new stores in the quarter, taking the network to 3,758 stores. Domestic business grew 22%, while international surged 97%. In theJewellery segment, around 21% growth, with 42 new stores bringing the total to 1,269. Furthermore, Tanishq, Mia, Zoya and beYon grew 20% together, while CaratLane stood out at 32% with 13 new stores. Mphasis Mphasis announced an agreement worth about £35.4 million with Social Security Scotland. The company will manage and maintain the platform that handles benefit applications, eligibility decisions and payments for around 2 million citizens. JSW Cement JSW Cement commissioned an additional 1 MTPA grinding unit in Nagaur, Rajasthan. This lifts the plant's capacity to 3.50 MTPA and the company's total grinding capacity to 25.1 MTPA, with clinker capacity standing at 9.74 MTPA including its joint venture. ALSO READJP Morgan’s festive picks: Why Titan, Lenskart, LG Electronics, Pidilite top the list The Big Event: RBI MPC The RBI Monetary Policy Committee's decision is due on October 7, which makes it the main reason traders will be glued to their screens. The stocks and sectors in focus include - Banks: ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank Insurers: ICICI Lombard, SBI Life and HDFC Life Rate-sensitive sectors: Real estate, automobiles and leveraged NBFCs The brokerage house Emkay in its report added, "We expect the RBI to kick off the rate hike cycle with a cautious 25bp increase, while retaining a neutral stance and signaling a higher-for-longer rate environment; a 50bp hike remains an outside risk as tighter global financial conditions increasingly shape the RBI's reaction function. Inflation is emerging as the key concern, with pressures broadening beyond food and our 2HFY27 forecasts running ~20bps above the RBI's projections." Meanwhile, FCNR-led excess liquidity continues to keep monetary conditions accommodative despite a tactical mix of sterilization tools, making liquidity management an ongoing challenge. The October policy should offer greater clarity on the RBI's sterilization strategy, with a further OMO sales announcement possible," said Emkay in its report. Investors must conduct their own independent due diligence and seek advice from a SEBI-registered financial advisor.

docs.title: BPCL, HPCL, IOC in focus: Morgan Stanley sees a 3-year refining upswing
docs.text: Morgan Stanley expects the earnings environment for Indian fuel retailers to remain supportive as refining margins improve, fuel prices recover and global product inventories stay tight. The global investment bank sees a three-year runway for the refining upcycle and says Indian refiners are in a favourable position as new capacity coming on stream is weighted towards diesel and jet fuel. Morgan Stanley’s latest India Energy update, titled Tracking Margins, says integrated margins should remain positive despite cooking gas-related losses, while stronger marketing margins and resilient fuel demand provide additional support. The brokerage prefers Hindustan Petroleum and Bharat Petroleum, with its industry coverage also including Indian Oil. ALSO READFrom 7.1% to 15.3%: HDFC Bank’s loan growth comeback is hard to ignore Morgan Stanley sees refining margins holding above historical levels Indian fuel retailers have continued to outperform the local market despite several energy shocks over the past five years, according to Morgan Stanley. The brokerage attributed the recent performance to greater confidence around earnings delivery, returns and the value of refining assets. Morgan Stanley report stated that, "Indian fuel retailers continue to outperform despite multiple energy shocks over the past five years. Their outperformance versus the local market over the last year reflects growing investor confidence in earnings delivery, returns, and the strategic value of refining assets." The brokerage expects integrated margins to remain positive even after accounting for cooking gas-related losses in September 2026. It also noted that Dubai crude remains below EBITDA breakeven levels of around $90 a barrel, while private fuel retailers have raised prices. Morgan Stanley said, "We expect integrated margins to remain positive this quarter even after factoring in cooking gas-related losses in Sept-26. Current margin trends continue to improve, with Dubai crude remaining below EBITDA breakeven levels at around $90 Private fuel retailers raised fuel prices by 4-5% last week and we have seen a rise in prices across CNG, natural gas and even commercial LPG." Tight global fuel inventories add to the support The supply-demand backdrop is also working in favour of refiners. Morgan Stanley said global fuel inventories remain close to 2022 lows, while limited additions to refining capacity and resilient demand should keep margins above historical mid-cycle levels. The brokerage expects Indian refiners to benefit from this environment as the country adds significant refining capacity at a time when diesel and jet fuel remain among the tighter parts of the global product slate. "Global fuel inventories remain near 2022 lows, while limited capacity additions and resilient demand should keep refining margins above historical mid-cycle levels," the Morgan Stanley analysts said. Indian refiners enter a favourable capacity cycle Morgan Stanley sees Indian refiners as unusual among global peers because the country is adding significant refining capacity during 2026-27. The new capacity is also expected to be weighted towards diesel and jet fuel, which the brokerage describes as the tightest segments of the barrel. This gives Indian refiners an opportunity to benefit from both higher capacity and a supportive product mix. The brokerage said, "Indian refiners are among the few globally adding significant refining capacity in 2026-27, with nearly half of incremental output skewed toward diesel and jet fuel, the tightest segments of the barrel. We see a three-year runway for the refining upcycle, with Indian refiners also benefiting from flexibility, and higher conversion yields." Morgan Stanley's view is therefore not limited to near-term marketing margins. Its thesis combines stronger refining economics with capacity additions, product flexibility and higher conversion yields. BPCL, HPCL emerge as Morgan Stanley’s preferred oil stocks Morgan Stanley explicitly said it prefers Hindustan Petroleum Corporation Ltd. and Bharat Petroleum within the Indian fuel-retailing space. Its industry coverage also includes Indian Oil. The brokerage uses separate sum-of-the-parts valuation frameworks for the three companies, assigning different enterprise value-to-EBITDA multiples to refining, fuel marketing, pipelines, petrochemicals and other businesses. Bharat Petroleum gets support from refining and marketing For Bharat Petroleum, Morgan Stanley values the refining and fuel-marketing businesses using 2028 estimated EBITDA multiples of 7 times each. The brokerage said these multiples are in line with global peers and are appropriate given the company's commodity exposure, EBITDA and margin outlook, debt quality and capital expenditure. The brokerage also applies a 25% discount to the market value of Bharat Petroleum’s listed investments because of market volatility risks. Among the factors that could strengthen the case, Morgan Stanley lists market-share gains in fuel retailing, faster completion of the Bina upgrade project and progress in the Mozambique asset. The risks include government control of fuel prices if crude prices rise sharply, a significant loss of market share in key fuels and delays in Bina and city gas projects that could lead to cost overruns. docs.title: 5 investment themes, 20 stocks: How to ride India’s next capex boom
docs.text: India’s investment landscape is expanding beyond traditional infrastructure such as roads, railways and defence into a much broader set of themes. The numbers give some sense of the scale. The FY27 Budget has allocated ₹12.2 lakh crore towards capital expenditure, while the defence allocation stands at ₹7.85 lakh crore. But government spending is only one part of the investment story. Private-sector investment is also moving into areas that were relatively small parts of India’s industrial landscape a few years ago. Companies are committing capital to semiconductors, power and transmission, data centres, nuclear energy, aerospace and electric vehicles. Government initiatives such as the Production Linked Incentive scheme have also encouraged companies to build capacity and invest in domestic manufacturing. As a result, the opportunity is becoming broader than government expenditure alone. Some of these themes are already visible in the market, while others are still taking shape. Against this backdrop, we look at five investment themes that could play an important role in shaping India’s next growth cycle, along with the stocks positioned around them. FE Stock Insights on WhatsApPGet instant alerts on high-conviction investment themes and fundamental deep dives—direct from Financial Express.Join now Theme #1: Power & Transmission, Renewable Energy, Energy Storage Systems India’s power requirement is changing rapidly. Manufacturing, data centres, railways, electric vehicles and urbanisation are all adding to electricity demand. In 2026, peak power demand reached a record 270.8 GW. The power sector added 52.5 GW of capacity in FY26, up from 34 GW in FY25. Renewables are becoming a larger part of this expansion. Of the capacity added in FY26, 39.7 GW came from renewable energy. As of July 31, 2026, India had crossed 300 GW of non-fossil fuel-based installed generation capacity, reaching 60% of its 2030 target of 500 GW. Non-fossil sources now account for around 54% of the country's total installed generation capacity. But adding generation capacity is only one part of the equation. The electricity also has to reach where it is needed. This is where a ₹1.6 lakh crore worth High Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) opportunity is expected to play a central role. The opportunity extends beyond HVDC to the broader transmission sector. The National Electricity Plan (2023-2032) projects peak power demand of 458 GW by 2032. The plan outlines an estimated ₹9.15 lakh crore investment in the transmission system. The transmission network is expected to expand from around 5 lakh circuit km in January 2026 to 6.48 lakh circuit km by 2032. Over the same period, transformation capacity is expected to rise from 1,407 GVA to 2,345 GVA. To capture these opportunities, these three companies are expanding their transformer capacity by up to 400%. The government has already started expanding this ecosystem. The proposed ₹1.86 lakh crore Green Energy Corridor is one example of the investment required to connect new renewable capacity to the grid. The opportunity is also extending beyond the grid itself. India's renewable expansion is creating a need for large-scale energy storage, including battery energy storage and pumped-storage projects. Nuclear power could add another layer to this investment cycle. Taken together, these developments point to a broader power-infrastructure opportunity. For investors, the focus is therefore not just on power generators, but on the companies supplying the equipment and systems needed to build, connect and manage India's expanding electricity network. Here are some of the stocks we covered recently that could ride this opportunity: #1 Tata Power: Integrated play with presence across power generation, transmission and renewable energy. #2 CG Power: Supplies transformers and critical power equipment #3 Power Grid: Direct beneficiary of transmission network expansion #4 Hitachi Energy: Benefits from grid modernisation and electrification demand You can read our entire coverage here… ALSO READIndia’s Rs 16 lakh crore data centre supercycle: 2 stocks connecting & powering the boom Theme #2: Semiconductors & Electronics: Building a New Manufacturing Ecosystem India’s electronics manufacturing push is gradually creating a wider ecosystem, spanning semiconductors, electronic components, specialised materials and chemicals. The government has been supporting this shift through the India Semiconductor Mission (ISM). ISM 1.0 came with a ₹76,000 crore outlay at a time when India has virtually no domestic semiconductor manufacturing base. The programme helped build the foundation needed for semiconductor design, fabrication and assembly and testing capabilities in the country. The recently approved ISM 2.0 has taken the planned government support to around ₹1.27 lakh crore. The second phase focuses on developing semiconductor equipment and materials in India, building indigenous semiconductor intellectual property and strengthening domestic and global supply chains. These pharma stocks, chemical players and fluorochemical companies are diversifying into semiconductor chemicals. Apart from this, due to increasing demand for ultra-clean water, water companies are also getting big opportunities in the semiconductor space. In addition to these two players, this hidden Murugappa Group company is also cashing in on the chip push. India’s electronics manufacturing growth is adding another layer to this theme. Mobile phone production has expanded sharply by 33X to ₹6.3 lakh crore, driven by government incentives and the PLI scheme.
